marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q015.takeaway: Carotid bifurcation lies at upper thyroid-cartilage border, approximately C3–C4.
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q015.displayText: The carotid bifurcation is at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, approximately C3-C4. The right common carotid arises from the brachiocephalic trunk and the left directly from the arch of aorta. In the neck, each is enclosed in the carotid sheath with the internal jugular vein and vagus nerve and divides into internal and external carotid arteries. Clinical points include carotid bifurcation stenosis/atherosclerosis, carotid sinus hypersensitivity and endarterectomy.
emphasis: upper border of the thyroid cartilage

rationales.a: The common carotid bifurcation lies at the upper, not lower, border of thyroid cartilage.
rationales.c: Cricothyroid membrane/cartilage is not the landmark; the source uses upper border of thyroid cartilage.
rationales.d: The bifurcation is not at the cricoid cartilage level.

marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q016.takeaway: Ascending pharyngeal artery is the medial ECA branch.
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q016.displayText: The only branch of the external carotid artery given from its medial side is the ascending pharyngeal artery. The external carotid begins at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage around C4 and gives superior thyroid, ascending pharyngeal, lingual, facial, occipital and posterior auricular arteries before terminating as maxillary and superficial temporal arteries.

rationales.a: Superior thyroid artery is an anterior ECA branch.
rationales.b: Facial artery is an anterior ECA branch.
rationales.d: Lingual artery is an anterior ECA branch; ascending pharyngeal is the single medial branch.

marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q017.takeaway: Internal carotid artery has no cervical branches.
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q017.displayText: The internal carotid artery gives no branches in the cervical region. It is the terminal branch of the common carotid beginning at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage.
emphasis: upper border of the thyroid cartilage

rationales.a: Pharyngeal branches arise from ECA, not cervical ICA.
rationales.b: Pterygoid branch belongs to petrous ICA, not cervical ICA.
rationales.c: Caroticotympanic branches arise from petrous ICA; no branch arises in cervical region.

marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q018.takeaway: Ophthalmic artery arises from cerebral ICA, not cavernous segment.
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q018.displayText: Cavernous sinus thrombosis may narrow the cavernous part of the internal carotid artery. Branches arising from the cavernous part include meningeal artery, inferior hypophyseal arteries and branches to the trigeminal ganglion. The ophthalmic artery is not a cavernous-part branch and therefore is not involved in the described lesion.

rationales.a: Meningeal artery is a cavernous ICA branch.
rationales.b: Inferior hypophyseal arteries and trigeminal ganglion branches can arise from cavernous segment.
rationales.d: Trigeminal ganglion branches are cavernous ICA branches; ophthalmic artery arises from cerebral ICA.

marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q019.takeaway: Dorsal nasal artery arises from ophthalmic, not facial artery.
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q019.displayText: The dorsal nasal artery is not a branch of the facial artery; it is a branch of the ophthalmic artery. The facial artery runs a tortuous course in the carotid triangle above the origin of the lingual artery and crosses the anterior border of masseter to reach the face. Source table: ascending palatine artery is accompanied by tonsillar nerve and is related to face; tonsillar artery by superior constrictor/inferior alveolar?; submental artery by lateral nasal artery; branch to submandibular gland by angular artery. (Some source table relationships are presentation-oriented and should be checked against the rendered source.)
emphasis: not a branch of the facial artery

rationales.a: Alar nasal branch is a facial artery branch and is affected by facial ligation.
rationales.b: Superior labial branch arises from facial artery and would be affected.
rationales.c: Premasseteric artery is a facial artery branch and would be affected; dorsal nasal comes from ophthalmic artery.

marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q020.takeaway: Pterygoid canal contains joined greater petrosal parasympathetic and deep petrosal sympathetic fibers.
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q020.displayText: The pterygoid canal is formed by fusion of postganglionic sympathetic fibers of the deep petrosal nerve and preganglionic parasympathetic fibers of the greater petrosal nerve. The nerve of the pterygoid canal (Vidian nerve) traverses this canal from the middle cranial fossa to the pterygopalatine fossa. It carries autonomic fibers ultimately distributed to lacrimal and nasal mucous glands; hence a fracture involving the canal can injure the greater and deep petrosal components.

rationales.a: Lesser petrosal nerve carries parasympathetic fibers toward otic ganglion, not through pterygoid canal.
rationales.c: Chorda tympani joins lingual nerve and carries taste/parasympathetic fibers but does not form Vidian nerve.
rationales.d: Lesser petrosal is not the preganglionic parasympathetic component of pterygoid canal; greater petrosal joins deep petrosal.

marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q021.takeaway: Artery of pterygoid canal is a pterygopalatine (third) maxillary artery branch.
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q021.displayText: The marked structure is the pterygoid canal. The artery of the pterygoid canal is a branch of the pterygopalatine (third) part of the maxillary artery. Branches of the pterygopalatine part include posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, greater palatine, pharyngeal, artery of pterygoid canal and sphenopalatine arteries.

rationales.a: Mandibular part of maxillary artery gives branches in infratemporal fossa, not artery of pterygoid canal.
rationales.b: Pterygoid part gives muscular branches; the pterygoid canal artery is from pterygopalatine part.
rationales.d: Petrous part refers to ICA segment, not a maxillary artery division.

marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q022.takeaway: External jugular vein forms from posterior auricular and posterior retromandibular veins.
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q022.displayText: The image shows distension of the external jugular vein. Its formative tributaries are the posterior auricular vein and the posterior division of the retromandibular vein. Facial/scalp venous drainage: superficial temporal and maxillary veins join to form retromandibular vein; its anterior division joins facial vein to form common facial vein draining into internal jugular; its posterior division joins posterior auricular vein to form external jugular vein, which drains into the subclavian vein.
emphasis: posterior division of the retromandibular vein

rationales.a: Facial vein is not a formative tributary of external jugular vein; facial drainage joins anterior retromandibular division.
rationales.c: Superficial temporal and maxillary veins unite to form retromandibular vein, not EJV directly.
rationales.d: Deep facial vein joins facial vein; EJV is formed by posterior auricular and posterior retromandibular veins.

marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q023.takeaway: Dangerous facial triangle includes midline upper lip and nose to nasal root.
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q023.displayText: The dangerous area of the face is the triangular area extending from the corners of the mouth to the bridge of the nose, including the nose and maxilla. Therefore the middle third of the upper lip is included. Facial vein communicates with cavernous sinus through superior ophthalmic vein and pterygoid venous plexus; facial infection can spread intracranially and cause cavernous sinus thrombosis.
emphasis: middle third of the upper lip

rationales.b: Middle third of lower lip falls below mouth corners and is outside the classic dangerous triangle.
rationales.c: Lateral lower lip is outside the triangular area extending from mouth corners to nasal bridge.
rationales.d: Periorbital area is not within the defined lower-face triangle.

marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q024.takeaway: Neck nodal level VI extends from hyoid to clavicle in anterior compartment.
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q024.displayText: The correct pair is level 6 - hyoid to clavicle. The source groups cervical lymph nodes by level: level 1 submental/submandibular; level 2 upper jugular; level 3 middle jugular; level 4 lower jugular; level 5 posterior triangle; level 6 anterior group; level 7 mediastinal. The accompanying diagram shows lateral-view neck node levels.

rationales.a: Level II is upper jugular region; it does not extend hyoid to clavicle.
rationales.b: Level IV covers lower jugular chain, approximately cricoid to clavicle, not hyoid to clavicle.
rationales.c: Level V follows posterior triangle and does not span anterior hyoid-to-clavicle interval.
